_link.title: I can explain the cause and role of transpiration and how the cohesion-tension mechanism drives water movement through the xylem

options.text: The evaporation of water from leaves through open stomata into the atmosphere
The absorption of water by roots from the soil
The transport of sugars through phloem
The process of photosynthesis in leaves

explanations.a: Correct. Transpiration is the movement of water through a plant from roots and its evaporation through the leaves into the atmosphere.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Water absorption by roots is a separate process. Transpiration refers to the evaporative loss of water from leaves.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Sugar transport through phloem is translocation, not transpiration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Photosynthesis is the production of sugar using light energy. Transpiration is the evaporation of water from leaves.

toLevel2.stem: What is cohesion in the context of water transport in plants?

options.text: The attraction between water molecules that causes them to stick together
The attraction between water and xylem walls
The evaporation of water from leaf surfaces
The active pumping of water by root cells

explanations.a: Correct. Cohesion is the sticking together of water molecules due to their polar nature, which helps maintain a continuous water column in the xylem.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The attraction between water and xylem walls is called adhesion, not cohesion.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Evaporation from leaves is transpiration, not cohesion.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Active pumping is not how xylem transport works. Cohesion is a property of water molecules.

options.text: The continuous column of water that forms inside the xylem as a result of evaporative water loss
A river that flows through the roots of plants
The flow of sugar through phloem tissue
The air current that moves through leaf pores

explanations.a: Correct. The transpiration stream is the continuous column of water pulled upward through the xylem, driven by the evaporation of water from the leaves.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The transpiration stream is inside the plant's xylem, not a river in the soil.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Sugar flow through phloem is a separate process. The transpiration stream refers to water in the xylem.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The transpiration stream is a water column in xylem, not an air current.

toLevel2.stem: What percentage of water absorbed by roots is lost through transpiration?

options.text: Over 97%
About 50%
Less than 10%
About 25%

explanations.a: Correct. Over 97% of water absorbed by roots is lost through transpiration. Only a very small amount is used for photosynthesis.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The figure is much higher than 50%. Over 97% is lost through transpiration.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Less than 10% would mean most water is retained. In reality, over 97% is lost.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Over 97% of absorbed water is lost, not just 25%.

toLevel2.stem: What is adhesion in the context of water transport?

options.text: The attraction between water molecules and the xylem cell walls
The attraction between water molecules and other water molecules
The force of root pressure pushing water upward
The process of water evaporating from leaves

explanations.a: Correct. Adhesion is the attraction between two different types of molecules — in this case, water molecules and the walls of xylem cells.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Attraction between water molecules is cohesion, not adhesion.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Root pressure is a separate mechanism. Adhesion is a property of water interacting with surfaces.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Water evaporating from leaves is transpiration, not adhesion.

toLevel2.stem: Transpiration is a passive process that requires no energy (ATP) from the plant.

distractor.explanation: This is true. Transpiration is driven by the evaporation of water from leaves and the physical properties of water (cohesion and adhesion). It requires no ATP from the plant.

toLevel2.stem: Most of the water in the transpiration stream is used for photosynthesis.

distractor.explanation: Only a very small amount of water in the transpiration stream is used for photosynthesis. Over 97% of absorbed water is lost through transpiration from the leaves.

toLevel2.stem: Transpiration creates a {{blank:1}} in the xylem that pulls water upward from the roots to the leaves.
{{blank:1}} is the attraction between water molecules, while {{blank:2}} is the attraction between water and xylem walls.
Transpiration is important because it transports minerals to leaves, provides water for {{blank:1}} and keeps the plant {{blank:2}}.

toLevel3.stem: How does transpiration create an upward pull on water in the xylem?

options.text: Water evaporating from leaf surfaces must be replaced, creating tension that pulls the water column upward through the xylem
The roots actively pump water upward to replace evaporated water
Gravity pulls water from leaves down through the xylem
Photosynthesis generates pressure that pushes water upward

explanations.a: Correct. As water evaporates from leaf surfaces through stomata, it creates a negative pressure (tension) at the top of the xylem. This tension pulls the continuous water column upward, drawing replacement water from the roots.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Roots generate some pressure, but it only reaches about 6.4 m. The main driving force is the transpiration pull from above.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Gravity pulls water downward. Transpiration works against gravity to pull water up.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Photosynthesis uses water but does not generate the pressure that drives transpiration.

toLevel3.stem: Why is cohesion essential for the transpiration stream to function?

options.text: Cohesion holds water molecules together so the column does not break when tension pulls it upward against gravity
Cohesion pushes water molecules apart to create flow
Cohesion prevents water from evaporating at the leaves
Cohesion only works in the roots, not in the xylem

explanations.a: Correct. Water molecules stick together due to cohesion (hydrogen bonds between polar molecules). This keeps the water column intact as tension from transpiration pulls it upward, preventing gaps from forming.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Cohesion causes attraction between water molecules, not repulsion.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Cohesion keeps the water column together inside the xylem; it does not prevent evaporation at the leaves.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Cohesion operates throughout the entire xylem column, from roots to leaves.

toLevel3.stem: What role does adhesion play in the transpiration stream?

options.text: Water adhering to xylem walls helps support the water column and assists in pulling water upward along the tube surface
Adhesion breaks the water column to allow air to enter
Adhesion pushes water away from xylem walls
Adhesion only occurs in the roots

explanations.a: Correct. Adhesion is the attraction between water molecules and the xylem wall surface. This helps support the water column against gravity and assists in drawing water upward along the tube walls.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Adhesion supports the water column, not breaks it.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Adhesion attracts water to the walls, not repels it.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Adhesion occurs along the entire length of the xylem, not just in roots.

toLevel3.stem: Why is it significant that transpiration is a passive process?

options.text: It means the plant can transport water over 100 m vertically without expending any metabolic energy on the process
It means the process occurs only at night
It means the plant can control the rate precisely
It means no water is lost from the plant

explanations.a: Correct. Plants lack a heart or pump, yet transpiration moves water over enormous distances using only evaporation and the physical properties of water. This is energetically free for the plant.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Transpiration occurs primarily during the day when stomata are open and conditions favour evaporation.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Being passive means the plant has limited direct control over transpiration rate (it can only adjust stomata opening).
explanations.d: Incorrect. Transpiration involves significant water loss — over 97% of absorbed water evaporates.

toLevel3.stem: Why is transpiration necessary despite causing the plant to lose over 97% of its absorbed water?

options.text: It is the driving force for water and mineral transport to the leaves, and it also provides cooling to prevent overheating
The plant does not actually need the lost water
Transpiration only occurs in emergencies
The 97% figure is inaccurate; plants retain most of their water

explanations.a: Correct. Despite the high water loss, transpiration is vital because it drives the transpiration stream that delivers water and minerals to leaves, provides water for photosynthesis and cools the plant through evaporative cooling.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The lost water was essential for creating the tension that drives the entire transport system.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Transpiration is a continuous process that occurs whenever stomata are open, not just in emergencies.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Over 97% water loss is well-documented. The plant absorbs water continuously through its roots to replace it.

toLevel3.stem: Why do water molecules exhibit cohesion?

options.text: Because water molecules are polar, with partial positive and negative charges that attract neighbouring molecules
Because water molecules are non-polar and repel each other
Because lignin in xylem walls forces water molecules together
Because the plant actively bonds water molecules using enzymes

explanations.a: Correct. Water molecules have a partial negative charge on the oxygen end and partial positive charges on the hydrogen ends. These opposite charges attract between neighbouring molecules, creating hydrogen bonds that hold water together (cohesion).
explanations.b: Incorrect. Water molecules are polar, not non-polar. Their polarity causes them to attract, not repel.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Lignin repels water (hydrophobic). Cohesion is an inherent property of water molecules, not caused by xylem walls.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Cohesion is a physical property of water due to its molecular structure, not an enzymatic process.

toLevel3.stem: Root pressure alone is sufficient to transport water to the top of a 115 m California redwood.

distractor.explanation: Root pressure can only push water up to about 6.4 metres. In a 115 m redwood, the transpiration pull combined with cohesion and adhesion is the mechanism that draws water to the canopy.

toLevel3.stem: Water evaporating from leaves creates {{blank:1}} in the xylem, and {{blank:2}} between water molecules prevents the column from breaking.
Water molecules are {{blank:1}}, with partial positive charges on hydrogen and partial negative charges on oxygen, which causes them to attract each other.
Transpiration is vital because it drives the transport of {{blank:1}} to the leaves and provides {{blank:2}} cooling for the plant.

toLevel4.stem: A celery stick is placed in coloured dye. The dye moves up the stem and into the leaves. If the leaves are then cut off, the dye stops moving. Explain why.

options.text: Without leaves, there is no evaporation to create the transpiration pull that draws water upward through the xylem
The celery dies immediately when leaves are removed
The dye is too heavy to move without leaves pushing it
Removing leaves blocks the xylem tubes

explanations.a: Correct. Transpiration from the leaves creates the tension that pulls water (and dye) upward. Without leaves, there is no evaporation, no tension and no upward pull, so the dye stops moving.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The celery does not die immediately. The dye stops because the driving force (transpiration) is removed.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The dye moves because of transpiration pull, not because leaves push it.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Removing leaves does not physically block the xylem. It removes the evaporation that drives flow.

toLevel4.stem: On a hot, dry day, transpiration rate increases significantly. Predict the effect on the water column in the xylem.

options.text: Greater tension develops in the xylem as water evaporates faster, pulling water upward more forcefully — but risking column breakage if cohesion is overcome
The water column becomes thicker and stronger
Water flows downward to the roots to escape the heat
The xylem cells expand to hold more water

explanations.a: Correct. Faster evaporation increases tension in the xylem. This pulls water up faster, but if tension exceeds the cohesive forces, the water column could break (cavitation), creating an air embolism.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The water column does not become thicker. Increased tension puts it under greater stress.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Water moves upward through the xylem, not downward. Increased transpiration increases upward pull.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Xylem cells are dead and rigid. They do not expand.

toLevel4.stem: If a plant were coated with a waterproof substance on all its leaf surfaces, what would happen to transpiration?

options.text: Transpiration would stop because water cannot evaporate through the sealed surface, removing the driving force for xylem transport
Transpiration would increase because the coating traps heat
The plant would absorb more water through its roots to compensate
Water would start evaporating through the stems instead

explanations.a: Correct. Sealing leaf surfaces prevents water evaporation. Without evaporation, no tension develops in the xylem and the transpiration stream stops. The plant would eventually suffer from lack of water and mineral delivery to leaves.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Even if heat is trapped, if water cannot evaporate through the sealed surface, there is no transpiration.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Root absorption is driven partly by the transpiration pull. Without transpiration, water uptake would decrease.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Stems are not significant sites of transpiration. Leaves are the primary evaporation surface.

toLevel4.stem: A California redwood is 115 m tall. How does the cohesion-tension mechanism transport water to the top against gravity?

options.text: Transpiration at the canopy creates tension that pulls the water column upward; cohesion keeps the column intact over the entire 115 m; adhesion supports the column against the xylem walls
Root pressure alone pushes water 115 m upward
The tree uses active transport to pump water up the trunk
Water flows upward because xylem tubes are pressurised like pipes

explanations.a: Correct. Evaporation at the canopy creates tension that pulls water upward. Cohesion between water molecules maintains the column as one continuous chain. Adhesion to xylem walls provides additional support. All three work together passively.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Root pressure reaches only about 6.4 m. It is insufficient for a 115 m tree.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Xylem transport is passive. There is no active pumping mechanism in xylem.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Xylem operates under negative pressure (tension/suction), not positive pressure.

toLevel4.stem: A plant wilts on a very hot day even though the soil is moist. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Transpiration rate exceeds the rate of water absorption by roots, creating a water deficit in the plant
The roots have stopped absorbing water because the soil is too wet
Cohesion has permanently broken down in the xylem
The stomata have closed, blocking water entry

explanations.a: Correct. On hot days, evaporation from leaves is very rapid. If transpiration outpaces root absorption, the plant loses more water than it gains, causing cells to lose turgor and the plant to wilt — even in moist soil.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Roots continue to absorb water from moist soil via osmosis. The problem is that transpiration is outpacing absorption.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Cohesion can temporarily break (cavitation), but in moist soil the issue is a rate mismatch between loss and uptake.
explanations.d: Incorrect. If stomata close, transpiration would decrease, which would reduce water loss, not cause wilting.

toLevel4.stem: How does transpiration help cool a plant on a hot day?

options.text: Evaporating water absorbs heat energy from the leaf surface, lowering the leaf temperature
Transpiration pumps cold water from deep roots to the leaves
The stomata release cold air from inside the leaf
Transpiration blocks sunlight from reaching the leaf

explanations.a: Correct. Evaporation is an endothermic process — it absorbs heat energy. When water evaporates from leaf surfaces during transpiration, it takes heat with it, cooling the leaf (evaporative cooling).
explanations.b: Incorrect. The water itself is not cold. Cooling occurs through the evaporation process, not water temperature.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Stomata release water vapour, not cold air. The cooling is from the evaporation process.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Transpiration does not block sunlight. It cools the leaf through evaporative heat loss.

toLevel4.stem: If the cohesive forces between water molecules were suddenly weakened, how would this affect a tall tree?

options.text: The water column in the xylem would break, forming air gaps that block water transport and cause the upper parts to wilt
Water would flow upward faster without cohesion slowing it down
The tree would grow taller because water is lighter without cohesion
Root pressure would increase to compensate

explanations.a: Correct. Cohesion holds the water column together against the tension of transpiration. Without it, the column would break, creating air bubbles (cavitation) that block xylem tubes and prevent water from reaching the canopy.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Cohesion does not slow water down; it holds the column together. Without it, the column breaks.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Weakened cohesion would impair water transport, harming the tree.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Root pressure is limited (~6.4 m) and cannot compensate for a broken water column in a tall tree.

toLevel4.stem: When leaves are removed from a celery stick in dye, the dye stops moving because there is no {{blank:1}} to create the tension that drives upward flow.
In a 115 m redwood, {{blank:1}} at the canopy creates tension, {{blank:2}} holds the water column together, and adhesion supports the column against the xylem walls.
A plant wilts on a hot day because the rate of {{blank:1}} exceeds the rate of water {{blank:2}} by the roots.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why transpiration is described as a 'necessary cost' for the plant.

options.text: The plant loses vast amounts of water (over 97%) but gains the essential benefit of water and mineral transport to leaves plus evaporative cooling
Transpiration has no cost because the plant does not need water
The cost is unnecessary because root pressure alone can supply water
Transpiration is entirely beneficial with no drawbacks

explanations.a: Correct. Transpiration is a trade-off: the plant must lose over 97% of absorbed water through evaporation, but this drives the entire transport system that delivers water and minerals to leaves and prevents overheating. Without it, the plant could not sustain its above-ground organs.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Water loss is a significant cost, especially in dry conditions where it can lead to wilting and death.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Root pressure only reaches ~6.4 m. For tall plants, transpiration is the essential mechanism.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The massive water loss is a real drawback, especially during drought.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'Transpiration is just water wasted by the plant.' Evaluate this claim.

options.text: It is flawed because transpiration drives the transport system that delivers water and minerals, provides water for photosynthesis and cools the plant — it is not wasted
It is correct because over 97% of water is lost
It is correct because the plant does not benefit from transpiration
It is flawed because plants do not lose water

explanations.a: Correct. While water is lost, transpiration is the essential driving force for xylem transport. Without it, minerals could not reach leaves, photosynthesis would be impaired and the plant could overheat. The water 'lost' performs vital work before it evaporates.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The percentage lost is high, but calling it 'wasted' ignores the essential functions transpiration serves.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The plant benefits enormously from transpiration-driven transport and cooling.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Plants do lose over 97% of absorbed water through transpiration.

toLevel5.stem: Compare the roles of root pressure and transpiration pull in water transport. Under what conditions is each most important?

options.text: Root pressure dominates at night or in short plants (up to ~6.4 m); transpiration pull dominates during the day in tall plants when evaporation is high
Root pressure is always stronger than transpiration pull
Transpiration pull only works in darkness
Both mechanisms work identically at all times

explanations.a: Correct. Root pressure provides a small upward push (~6.4 m max) and is more significant at night when transpiration is low. During the day, evaporation creates transpiration pull that dominates, pulling water far beyond root pressure's limit.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Root pressure is relatively weak (6.4 m max). Transpiration pull can move water over 100 m.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Transpiration pull is strongest during the day when light, heat and wind promote evaporation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Their relative contributions depend on time of day, plant size and environmental conditions.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate why the cohesion-tension model is widely accepted as the mechanism for water transport in tall plants.

options.text: It explains how water moves passively over 100 m using only evaporation and the physical properties of water, consistent with the observed absence of energy-dependent pumps in xylem
It is accepted because no other explanation has been proposed
It requires active transport, which matches observations
It only works for plants under 10 m tall

explanations.a: Correct. The cohesion-tension model elegantly explains long-distance passive transport: transpiration creates tension, cohesion maintains the water column and adhesion supports it. This matches observations that xylem cells are dead (no pumps) yet water reaches canopies over 100 m high.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Alternative hypotheses have been proposed, but the cohesion-tension model is best supported by evidence.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The model specifically explains passive transport. Xylem cells are dead and cannot perform active transport.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The model works for plants of all heights, from small shrubs to 115 m redwoods.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse the consequence of cavitation (water column breakage) in a xylem vessel and how the plant might cope.

options.text: Cavitation blocks water transport in that vessel; the plant copes by having multiple parallel xylem vessels and tracheids that can bypass the blocked column
Cavitation has no effect because the plant repairs the break instantly
Cavitation strengthens the water column
The plant dies immediately from any cavitation event

explanations.a: Correct. When a water column breaks, an air bubble fills the gap, blocking that vessel. Plants have many parallel xylem vessels and tracheids (with pits that limit bubble spread), providing alternative pathways for water transport.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Dead xylem cells cannot repair themselves. However, the plant can grow new xylem over time.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Cavitation weakens transport by blocking the vessel with air.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A single cavitation event affects one vessel. Redundancy in xylem pathways protects the plant.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse how transpiration connects the root system, shoot system and the atmosphere in a continuous pathway.

options.text: Roots absorb soil water → xylem transports it through stem → water evaporates from leaves into atmosphere, creating a continuous flow driven by the gradient from wet soil to dry air
The atmosphere pushes water into the plant through the leaves
Each system operates independently with no connection
Water moves from the atmosphere into the plant and down to the roots

explanations.a: Correct. Transpiration creates a continuous pathway: soil → root hair cells → root cortex → xylem → stem → leaf mesophyll → stomata → atmosphere. The water potential gradient from wet soil to dry air drives the entire system.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Water moves from the plant into the atmosphere (evaporation), not from the atmosphere into the plant.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The systems are fundamentally connected by the transpiration stream.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Water flows upward from soil through the plant and out through leaves, not from atmosphere downward.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that plants would be more efficient if they could transport water without losing any through transpiration. Evaluate this reasoning.

options.text: It is flawed because transpiration IS the driving force; without evaporation there is no tension to pull water upward, so eliminating transpiration would stop transport entirely
It is correct because plants waste too much water
It is correct because root pressure alone could replace transpiration
It is flawed because plants never lose water

explanations.a: Correct. The student misunderstands cause and effect. Transpiration (water loss) is not a side effect of transport — it IS the mechanism that creates the tension pulling water upward. Without it, there is no driving force for the transpiration stream.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While water loss is high, it is not 'waste' — it is the mechanism that drives the entire transport system.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Root pressure only reaches ~6.4 m and cannot replace transpiration for tall plants.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Plants do lose significant water through transpiration.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why adhesion is particularly important in narrow xylem vessels like tracheids compared to wider vessel elements.

options.text: In narrow tubes, a greater proportion of water molecules are in contact with the walls, so adhesive forces have a proportionally larger effect on supporting the water column
Adhesion is only important in vessel elements, not tracheids
Narrow tubes have no adhesion
Adhesion weakens in narrow tubes

explanations.a: Correct. In narrow tracheids, the surface area of wall contact relative to water volume is higher. This means adhesion (water-to-wall attraction) has a proportionally greater effect in supporting the water column, similar to how a thin capillary tube draws water higher than a wide one.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Adhesion operates in both cell types but has a proportionally greater effect in narrower tracheids.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Adhesion occurs in all tubes where water contacts the wall, including narrow ones.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Adhesion per unit of wall area remains the same. Its relative contribution increases in narrower tubes.

toLevel5.stem: Transpiration is the {{blank:1}} force for xylem transport, not a side effect; without evaporation there would be no {{blank:2}} to pull water upward.
The cohesion-tension model explains passive transport over 100 m using only {{blank:1}} and the physical properties of water, with no need for {{blank:2}} from the plant.
